standard_text: Understand that solutions to a system of two linear equations correspond to the point(s) of intersection of their graphs; solve and approximate solutions of a system by graphing (and interpret whether a system has one solution, no solution, or infinitely many).

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to solve a system of two linear equations by graphing: the solution is the point where the two lines intersect, and the graph also tells whether there is one solution, no solution, or infinitely many. The on-grade work moves from counting solutions on a given graph, to reading or approximating the intersection point, to graphing both lines from y = mx + b form and confirming the crossing point in both equations. Students who struggle here usually carry gaps from well below grade eight, most often shaky point plotting and weak substitution. Intervention should start with those foundations, rebuild the grade seven skills of graphing a proportional relationship as a line and solving two-step equations, and only then return to systems. Every candidate answer can be tested by substituting it into both equations.

steps.rationale: The conceptual entry: read a graph and decide how many solutions the system has — one (lines cross), none (parallel), infinitely many (same line). This settles what 'solution' means before any point is found.

A solution must lie on BOTH lines, so it must satisfy BOTH equations. Checking a candidate (x, y) by substitution into each equation is the verification spine that makes every later 'find the solution' honest.

Given the graph, read the intersection point as the solution — and approximate it when the crossing falls between gridlines. This is the Approaching-band expectation and where the coordinate-swap error surfaces.

Reverse the flow: from two equations in y = mx + b form, plot both lines and find where they meet. This is the At-band capstone that requires the graphing mechanic and reporting the full ordered pair.

Given a system, determine the solution (or the coordinate plane that shows it) and confirm it by substitution. Distinguishing the true point from a reversed or sign-flipped one proves the intersection is understood, not guessed.
The Above-band synthesis: estimate the solution of a real-world system from its graph and interpret the intersection as a break-even point — which option is better before it and after it.

skills.name: Plot and name points on the coordinate plane

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point from an ordered pair and name the ordered pair for a plotted point in the first quadrant, moving across first and up second.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot (3, 5), how far do you go across, and how far up?

skills.i_do_script: An ordered pair is a set of directions: the first number tells how far to walk across from 0, and the second tells how far to climb up. Watch (3, 5): I start at the origin, walk 3 spaces to the right along the bottom axis, then climb 5 spaces up, and put my dot there. The order matters: (3, 5) and (5, 3) are two different dots, because walking 5 and climbing 3 lands somewhere else. To name a plotted point, I do the same walk in reverse: count across to get the first number, then count up to get the second.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the order, going up first and across second
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 5) by going up 3 and across 5, landing on (5, 3)
canonical_error.why: The first number in an ordered pair is always the across move and the second is the up move. Swapping them lands on a different point.

skills.item_template: An ordered pair in the first quadrant. Student plots the point, names a plotted point, or describes the across and up moves. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: To plot (3, 5), how far across and how far up do you go?
A point sits 4 across and 2 up from the origin. Write its ordered pair.
Are (2, 6) and (6, 2) the same point?
sample_items.answer: No, the across and up moves are different

sample_items.stem: What point is at the origin, where the two axes cross?
To plot (0, 4), how far across do you go?
sample_items.answer: 0 across, so the point sits on the up axis, 4 up

sample_items.stem: A point sits 7 across and 0 up. Write its ordered pair.
Which number in (5, 1) tells the up move?
A point sits 1 across and 6 up. Write its ordered pair.

redirect_script.stop: Which number is the across move, the first or the second?
redirect_script.prompt: Start at the origin. Walk across by the first number, then climb up by the second. Say 'across, then up' as you move your finger.
redirect_script.praise: You walked across first and up second, that is exactly how the pair works.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers naming a point: across first, up second.
The point (0, 0) where the two axes cross; every walk starts there.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 coordinate graphing with a floor grid or geoboard (walk across, then up, from the origin).

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant grid from 0 to 6 on both axes. Circle the origin.
To plot (3, 5), where do we start, and which way do we move first?
Start at the origin. Walk 3 spaces across, then climb 5 spaces up, and mark the dot. The pair reads across, then up.
If a student climbs 3 first, plot both (3, 5) and (5, 3) and ask if they are the same dot.
Your turn: plot (4, 2) and tell me each move as you make it.

skills.name: Use substitution to decide whether a value makes an equation true

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute a given number for the variable in a one-step equation and decide whether the equation becomes true.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Does x = 4 make x + 3 = 7 true? How do you check?

skills.i_do_script: An equation is a claim, and substituting a number tests whether the claim is true. Watch: does x = 4 make x + 3 = 7 true? I replace x with 4 and compute the left side: 4 + 3 = 7. The two sides match, so x = 4 makes it true. Now test x = 5 in the same equation: 5 + 3 = 8, but the right side says 7. The sides do not match, so x = 5 does not make it true. A value only works if both sides come out equal.

canonical_error.pattern: Says a value works without computing both sides, or computes and ignores the mismatch
canonical_error.example: Tests x = 5 in x + 3 = 7, gets 8, and still says yes because 5 is close
canonical_error.why: True means the two sides are exactly equal after substituting. Close is not equal; if the sides differ at all, the value does not make the equation true.

skills.item_template: A one-step equation and a candidate value. Student substitutes, computes both sides, and answers yes or no. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Does x = 4 make x + 3 = 7 true?
Does x = 6 make 2x = 12 true?
Does x = 5 make x + 3 = 7 true?
Does x = 3 make 12 - x = 9 true?
Does x = 4 make 3x = 15 true?
Does x = 10 make x/2 = 5 true?
Does x = 7 make x - 2 = 5 true?
Does x = 2 make 8x = 18 true?

redirect_script.stop: What did each side come out to after you substituted?
redirect_script.prompt: Replace the variable with the number, compute the side it sits in, and compare it to the other side. Yes only if the two sides are exactly equal.
redirect_script.praise: You computed both sides and compared them, that is a real check.

vocabulary.definition: Replace a variable with a number, then compute.
A value that makes the equation true when substituted in.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 6 equations as balance claims (a pan balance picture: both sides must weigh the same).

worked_example_script.text: Draw a pan balance. Write x + 3 on the left pan and 7 on the right pan.
If x is 4, what does the left pan weigh? Does it balance the 7?
4 + 3 = 7, so the pans balance: x = 4 makes the equation true. Try x = 5: the left pan weighs 8 and tips down, so 5 does not work.
If a student says 5 works because it is close, point at the tipped balance: close does not balance.
Your turn: does x = 6 make 2x = 12 true? Show both sides.

skills.name: Graph a proportional relationship and read points as rate statements

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot the line for a proportional relationship from its unit rate, and read a point (x, y) as a statement about the situation, including (1, r) as the unit rate.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Apples cost 3 dollars per pound. What points would the cost graph pass through for 0, 1, and 2 pounds?

skills.i_do_script: A proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin, and the unit rate tells how fast it climbs. Watch: apples cost 3 dollars per pound. Zero pounds costs 0 dollars, so the line starts at (0, 0). One pound costs 3 dollars, point (1, 3). Two pounds costs 6 dollars, point (2, 6). I plot those points, and they line up, so I draw the line through them. Every point on the line is a statement: (4, 12) says 4 pounds cost 12 dollars, and the point (1, 3) always shows the unit rate.

canonical_error.pattern: Plots points with the coordinates reversed, or starts the line somewhere other than the origin
canonical_error.example: For 3 dollars per pound, plots (3, 1) instead of (1, 3), or starts the line at (0, 3)
canonical_error.why: The across value is the input (pounds) and the up value is the output (dollars), so 1 pound at 3 dollars is (1, 3). A proportional relationship always includes (0, 0) because zero of the input costs zero.

skills.item_template: A real-world unit rate (whole number or simple fraction). Student names points the line passes through, plots the line, or reads a point as a statement. Numeric or short response.

sample_items.stem: Apples cost 3 dollars per pound. Name the points for 0, 1, and 2 pounds.
A bike rides 8 miles per hour. What point shows the distance after 3 hours?
The point (1, 5) is on the graph of a proportional relationship. What is the unit rate?
Why does the graph of every proportional relationship pass through (0, 0)?
sample_items.answer: Zero of the input gives zero of the output

sample_items.stem: A graph of cost per pound passes through (2, 9). What does that point say?
Water fills at 4 gallons per minute. Name the points for 1, 2, and 5 minutes.
A proportional graph passes through (4, 10). What is the unit rate?
Pencils cost 2 dollars each. Which point is on the cost graph: (2, 1) or (1, 2)?

redirect_script.stop: Which axis is the input, and which is the output?
redirect_script.prompt: Start at (0, 0). For each 1 across, climb by the unit rate. Then read any point as a sentence: across amount of input gives up amount of output.
redirect_script.praise: You anchored at the origin and climbed by the rate, that is the line drawn right.

vocabulary.definition: A relationship where the output is always the same multiple of the input; its graph is a line through the origin.
The output for exactly 1 of the input; on the graph it is the point (1, r).

worked_example_script.text: Draw a grid with pounds across and dollars up. Say: apples cost 3 dollars per pound.
What does 0 pounds cost? 1 pound? 2 pounds? Where do those points go?
Plot (0, 0), (1, 3), and (2, 6). They line up, so draw the line through them. The point (1, 3) is the unit rate: 1 pound, 3 dollars.
If a student plots (3, 1), ask which axis holds pounds. Is it 3 pounds for 1 dollar, or 1 pound for 3 dollars?
Your turn: a car goes 5 miles per minute of the ride. Name three points and sketch the line.

practice_problems.stem: A proportional graph always passes through which point?
practice_problems.answer: (0, 0), the origin

practice_problems.stem: Bananas cost 2 dollars per pound. What point shows the cost of 1 pound?
A printer prints 6 pages per minute. Name the points for 0, 1, and 3 minutes, then sketch the line.
practice_problems.answer: (0, 0), (1, 6), (3, 18); a line through the origin climbing 6 per 1

practice_problems.stem: A proportional graph passes through (1, 4). What point is directly above 5 on the across axis?
A graph of miles per hour passes through (2, 12). What is the unit rate, and what point shows it?
practice_problems.answer: 6 miles per hour; (1, 6)

practice_problems.stem: Grapes cost 2.50 dollars per pound. What does the point (4, 10) on the cost graph say?
practice_problems.answer: 4 pounds cost 10 dollars

practice_problems.stem: Two workers are graphed on one grid: Ana at 3 walls per day and Ben at 5 walls per day. Whose line is steeper, and where do the two lines meet?
practice_problems.answer: Ben's line is steeper; both lines pass through (0, 0), so they meet only at the origin

practice_problems.stem: Milk costs 4 dollars per gallon. Jo plotted the cost graph through (0, 0) and (4, 1). Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Jo reversed the coordinates. One gallon costs 4 dollars, so the point is (1, 4), not (4, 1). The line goes through (0, 0), (1, 4), (2, 8).

activities.title: Climb by the Rate
materials: Grid paper
Rate cards (3 dollars per pound, 5 miles per hour, 2 pages per minute)
Counters
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair draws axes and labels them with the card's input and output.
2. Place a counter at (0, 0) and say why the line starts there.
3. Step the counter: 1 across, up by the rate. Mark a point at each step and say the sentence, like 2 pounds cost 6 dollars.
4. Draw the line through the marks and circle (1, r) as the unit rate point.
5. Trade grids and read three points off a partner's line as sentences.

activities.title: Rate, Point, Sentence
materials: Card deck: rate cards, point cards, and sentence cards
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each rate to the point (1, r) that shows it and to a sentence one of its points makes.
3. To claim a match, say where the line starts and how it climbs.
4. Two decoy point cards have reversed coordinates; set them aside and explain why they are wrong.

strategy_links.why: Stepping a counter 1 across and up by the rate makes the line's climb concrete before slope language appears.
Saying each point as a sentence out loud keeps the across and up values attached to their meanings, which blocks the coordinate swap.
The reversed-point error is precise and plottable, ideal for a find-and-fix.

questioning_prompts: Why does the line start at (0, 0)?
For each 1 across, how far up does the line climb?
What sentence does the point (2, 6) say in this situation?
Which point on the line shows the unit rate?
If the rate were bigger, what would change about the line?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plots the rate point with the coordinates reversed, like (3, 1) for 3 dollars per pound.
misconception_redirects.say: Read the axes first: pounds across, dollars up. One pound costs 3 dollars, so go 1 across and 3 up.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched each number to its axis, so the point tells the truth.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student starts the line above the origin, at (0, r).
misconception_redirects.say: What does zero pounds cost? Zero input gives zero output, so the line must pass through (0, 0).
misconception_redirects.praise: You anchored the line at the origin, that is what proportional means.

quick_checks.prompt: A drink costs 2 dollars per bottle. Name the points for 0, 1, and 4 bottles.
quick_checks.look_for: (0, 0), (1, 2), (4, 8), with the count across and the cost up.

quick_checks.prompt: A proportional graph passes through (3, 12). What is the unit rate?
quick_checks.look_for: 4 per 1, found by dividing 12 by 3; the point (1, 4).

worked_solution.stem: Apples cost 3 dollars per pound. Graph the cost and name the point for 4 pounds.
worked_solution.answer: A line through (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 6); the point for 4 pounds is (4, 12).

steps.annotation: Zero input gives zero output, so the line starts at the origin.
The unit rate point: 1 across, 3 up.
Each step across climbs 3 more; draw the line through the points.
Read the point as a sentence: 4 pounds cost 12 dollars.

faded_example.stem: A hose fills 4 gallons per minute. Graph the amount filled and name the point for 5 minutes.
faded_example.answer: A line through (0, 0), (1, 4), (2, 8); the point for 5 minutes is (5, 20).

steps.annotation: The line starts at the origin.
The unit rate point: 1 across, 4 up.
Name one more point and draw the line.
Find the point for 5 minutes and say it as a sentence.

sentence_starters: The line starts at (0, 0) because zero ___ gives zero ___.
The point (___ , ___) says that ___ of the input gives ___ of the output.

skills.name: Solve two-step equations of the form px + q = r

prerequisite_skill.description: Solve equations like 2x + 3 = 11 by undoing the addition first and the multiplication second, then check by substitution.

skills.i_do_script: A two-step equation wraps x in two operations, and I unwrap them in reverse order. Watch 2x + 3 = 11: the x was multiplied by 2, then 3 was added. I undo the addition first: subtract 3 from both sides, leaving 2x = 8. Then I undo the multiplication: divide both sides by 2, so x = 4. Last, I check by substitution: 2 times 4 plus 3 is 11, so x = 4 is right. Both sides get the same move every time, or the balance breaks.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides before subtracting, or applies a move to only one side
canonical_error.example: For 2x + 3 = 11, divides only 11 by 2 to get x + 3 = 5.5, or subtracts 3 from the left side only
canonical_error.why: The equation is a balance: every move must hit both full sides. Undo in reverse order, the added number first, then the multiplier, and the check by substitution catches any slip.

skills.item_template: An equation px + q = r with integer p, q and a clean solution. Student solves for x and checks by substitution. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: Solve: 2x + 3 = 11
Solve: 3x - 5 = 10
Solve: 4x + 1 = 9
Solve: 5x - 2 = 18
Solve: 2x + 7 = 7
Solve: 6x + 4 = 22
Solve: 3x + 2 = 20
Solve: 4x - 6 = 10

redirect_script.stop: Which operation do you undo first, and did both sides get the move?
redirect_script.prompt: Undo the added or subtracted number first, on both sides. Then divide both sides by the multiplier. Finish by substituting your answer back in.
redirect_script.praise: You undid in reverse order and kept both sides balanced, that is the whole method.

vocabulary.definition: The operation that undoes another: subtraction undoes addition, division undoes multiplication.
An equation stays true only when every move is made to both full sides.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a pan balance: two x-bags and 3 unit chips on the left pan, 11 chips on the right. Write 2x + 3 = 11 underneath.
What can we remove from BOTH pans without tipping the balance?
Take 3 chips off each pan: 2x = 8. Two bags weigh 8, so split both pans in half: one bag weighs 4. x = 4, and the check 2(4) + 3 = 11 confirms it.
If a student divides 11 by 2 first, point at the pans: the 3 chips are still sitting there, so the bags do not own the whole 11.
Your turn: solve 3x + 2 = 14 and check your answer.

practice_problems.stem: Solve: x + 5 = 12
Solve: 3x = 15
Solve: 2x + 3 = 15
Solve: 4x - 7 = 13
Solve: 5x + 2 = 32
Solve 3x - 4 = 11, then check your answer by substitution.
Solve: 7 = 2x - 5
Sam solved 2x + 6 = 14. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Sam divided by 2 before removing the 6, and he only divided part of the left side. Subtract 6 first: 2x = 8, so x = 4. Check: 2(4) + 6 = 14.

activities.title: Bags and Chips Balance
materials: Paper bags or cups labeled x
Counters or chips
A drawn pan balance mat
activities.instructions:
1. Build 2x + 3 = 11: two bags and 3 chips on the left mat, 11 chips on the right.
2. Remove 3 chips from EACH side and say why the balance holds.
3. Split both sides into two equal groups: one bag matches 4 chips, so x = 4.
4. Check by refilling: put 4 chips in each bag and count the left side to 11.
5. Repeat with 3x + 2 = 14 and 4x - 1 = 11, always saying: same move, both sides.

activities.title: Whose Balance Broke?
materials: Worked-solution slips, half correct and half with one bad move
activities.instructions:
1. Deal the slips face down.
2. Flip one at a time: decide whether every move hit both sides and came in the right order.
3. For each broken slip, name the bad move (divided too early, or one side only) and fix it.
4. Verify each fix by substituting the answer back into the original equation.

content.error_step: Divided the 2x by 2 without dividing the whole left side and the right side properly, before removing the 6
content.why: Dividing must hit both full sides, and the added 6 has to come off first: 2x = 8, x = 4.

strategy_links.why: Bags and chips on a balance make undo-in-reverse-order visible before it becomes a rule.
Thinking aloud, what happened to x and what undoes it, makes the order of moves audible and checkable.
Dividing too early is a stable error; finding and fixing it in shown work confronts it directly.

questioning_prompts: What two things happened to x in this equation?
Which operation do you undo first, and why that one?
Did both sides get the same move?
How can you prove your answer is right without asking me?
What would go wrong if you divided before subtracting?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides by the coefficient before removing the added number.
misconception_redirects.say: Look at the balance: the extra chips are still on the pan, so the bags do not own the whole total. Take the chips off both sides first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You cleared the added number first, so the divide came out clean.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student applies a move to one side only.
misconception_redirects.say: An equation is a balance. If you take 3 off the left, the right tips unless you take 3 off it too. Same move, both sides.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept both sides matched, so the equation stayed true.

quick_checks.look_for: x = 4, subtracting 5 first. An answer of 6.5 or 9 means the student divided early or moved one side only.

steps.annotation: x was multiplied by 2, then 3 was added; undo in reverse order.
Subtract 3 from both sides.
Divide both sides by 2.
Substitute back; both sides match, so x = 4 is correct.
x was multiplied by 3, then 4 was subtracted; undo in reverse order.
Add 4 to both sides.
Divide both sides by 3.
Check by substituting your answer back in.

sentence_starters: First I undo the ___ by ___ on both sides.
I know x = ___ is right because substituting it gives ___ on both sides.

skills.name: Determine the number of solutions of a system from its graph
skills.i_do_script: The number of solutions a system has is how many points its two lines SHARE -- and you can see it before you memorize anything. Graph both lines: if they cross once, one solution (one shared point). If they run parallel -- same steepness, different starting heights -- they never touch: no solution. If both equations draw the exact same line, every point is shared: infinitely many. The symbol shortcut just reads that picture off the equations: different slopes cross once; same slope with different y-intercepts is parallel; same slope AND same intercept is the same line. When the shortcut feels like a coin flip, draw three quick points of each line and look.

canonical_error.pattern: Decides the number of solutions from the number of lines or how steep they look, not from how many points the lines share
canonical_error.example: Sees two lines and answers 'two solutions,' or sees non-crossing parallel lines and answers 'one solution' instead of 'no solution'
canonical_error.why: The student hasn't connected 'solution' to 'shared point.' One solution = the lines cross once; no solution = parallel lines that never meet; infinitely many = the same line, which shares every point.

skills.item_template: A system in y = mx + b form (graph provided or described). Student states one / none / infinitely many by comparing slopes and intercepts. MC.

sample_items.stem: How many solutions does this system have?  y = 2x + 1  and  y = -x + 4
sample_items.distractor_logic: Different slopes (2 and -1) mean the lines cross once, at (1, 3). 'Two solutions' counts the lines.

sample_items.stem: How many solutions does this system have?  y = 3x + 2  and  y = 3x - 1
sample_items.distractor_logic: Same slope 3, different intercepts (2 vs -1): parallel, never cross.

sample_items.stem: How many solutions does this system have?  y = 9x  and  y = 9x - 7
sample_items.distractor_logic: Same slope 9, different intercepts (0 vs -7): parallel lines.

sample_items.stem: How many solutions does this system have?  y = -2x + 5  and  y = -2x + 5
sample_items.distractor_logic: Identical slope AND intercept: the same line, so every point is shared.

redirect_script.stop: How many points do the two lines actually share?
redirect_script.prompt: Compare the slopes and the y-intercepts. Different slopes cross once (one solution). Same slope but different b means parallel (no solution). Same slope AND same b is one line (infinitely many). Count shared points, not lines.
redirect_script.praise: You compared slopes and intercepts to count the shared points — that's how the graph tells you the number of solutions.

vocabulary.definition: Two linear equations considered together; its solution is the point(s) both lines share.
The point where two lines cross; the solution to the system.
Lines with the same slope but different y-intercepts; they never cross, so the system has no solution.

worked_example_script.text: Plot a few points of y = (1/2)x + 2 (marked from (0,2)) and y = (1/2)x - 1 (from (0,-1)): both climb 1 for every 2 across.
Both lines climb at the same rate but start at different heights. Will they ever meet? So how many points do they share?
They never meet -- same climb, different starting heights means the gap between them never closes. Zero shared points: no solution.
Write 'How many solutions?  y = (1/2)x + 2  and  y = (1/2)x + 2.'
Compare the slopes. Now compare the y-intercepts. What do you notice?
Same slope 1/2 and same intercept 2 — it's the exact same line, so infinitely many solutions.
If a student says 'two solutions,' ask 'are you counting lines, or the points where they cross?'
Your turn: y = -3x + 1 and y = -3x + 6 — how many solutions?

practice_problems.stem: Two lines cross at exactly one point. How many solutions does the system have?
practice_problems.answer: One solution.

practice_problems.stem: Lines with the same slope but different y-intercepts are called what, and how many solutions?
practice_problems.answer: Parallel; no solution.

practice_problems.stem: How many solutions?  y = 4x - 2  and  y = 4x - 2
practice_problems.answer: Infinitely many (same line).

practice_problems.stem: How many solutions?  y = 2x + 3  and  y = -x + 3
practice_problems.answer: One solution (different slopes, cross at (0, 3)).

practice_problems.stem: Maya judged the number of solutions. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Maya wrote: 'There are two lines, so there are two solutions.'
practice_problems.answer: Maya counted the lines, not the shared points. Both lines have slope 5 but different intercepts (1 and -4), so they are parallel and never cross: the system has NO solution.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: counting lines instead of intersection points.

practice_problems.stem: How many solutions?  y = 9x  and  y = 9x - 7
practice_problems.answer: No solution (parallel).

practice_problems.stem: Write a second equation so that y = 2x + 5 forms a system with NO solution.
practice_problems.answer: Any line with slope 2 and a different intercept, e.g. y = 2x + 1 (parallel).
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own; must keep slope, change b.

practice_problems.stem: Two lines have different slopes. Explain why the system must have exactly one solution.
practice_problems.answer: Different slopes are not parallel, so the lines head in different directions and meet at exactly one point — one shared point means one solution.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why; connects slope to intersection count.

activities.title: Graph One of Each
materials: Grid paper (or the grid-paper printable)
Three system cards: one crossing, one parallel, one same-line
activities.instructions:
1. Each group graphs all three systems, one per grid, plotting three points per line.
2. For each grid, COUNT the shared points: one crossing, zero, or 'every point.' Label each grid with its count.
3. Now look back at the equations: what do the slopes and intercepts look like in each case?
4. Groups write the rule themselves: 'different slopes → ___; same slope, different intercept → ___; same everything → ___.'
5. Debrief trap: why can 'same slope' NEVER mean one solution? (Parallel lines can't cross once -- they either never touch or are the same line.)

activities.title: One, None, or Infinitely Many
materials: Card set of 8 systems written in y = mx + b form
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each system card into 'One solution,' 'No solution,' or 'Infinitely many solutions.'
2. For each card, underline the two slopes and the two y-intercepts.
3. Say the rule you used: different slopes = one; same slope, different b = none; same slope and b = infinitely many.
4. Debrief: which two cases are easy to mix up, and how do the intercepts tell them apart?

activities.title: Count the Crossings
materials: Slip with Maya's two-solutions claim
activities.instructions:
1. Read Maya's claim that y = 5x + 1 and y = 5x - 4 has 'two solutions' because there are two lines.
2. Compare the two slopes, then the two y-intercepts.
3. Decide how many points the lines share and state the correct number of solutions.
4. Write the rule for reading solution count from slopes and intercepts.

skills.name: Identify or approximate the solution of a system from a given graph
skills.i_do_script: Two lines cross where they are at the same height at the same moment -- same x AND same y on both lines at once -- and naming that spot means saying how far ACROSS first, then how far UP. When a graph of a system is given, the solution is the point where the two lines cross — I read its x first (how far across) and its y second (how far up). Watch two lines that meet at the point 2 across and 3 up: the solution is (2, 3), not (3, 2). When the crossing lands between the gridlines, I estimate — if it looks a little past 0 across and about 2 and a third up, I'd say roughly (0.7, 2.3). The best answer is the ordered pair closest to where the lines actually meet.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the intersection with x and y swapped, or reports where a line crosses an axis instead of where the two lines meet
canonical_error.example: The lines cross at (0.7, 2.3) but the student writes (2.3, 0.7), reversing the coordinates
canonical_error.why: The solution is the (x, y) of the crossing point: x first (across), y second (up). Swapping the order — or reading a single line's axis-crossing — names a point that isn't the shared point.

skills.name: Graph a system of two equations and find the solution
skills.i_do_script: A slope's sign tells the pencil which way to travel: plug a couple of x-values into y = -x + 5 and you get 5, 4, 3 -- falling, not rising. A negative slope is a downhill walk as you move right. To solve a system by graphing, I graph BOTH lines from their y = mx + b form, then find where they cross. Watch y = 2x - 1 and y = -x + 5. Line 1 starts at (0, -1) and rises 2 for every 1 right. Line 2 starts at (0, 5) and FALLS 1 for every 1 right (the slope is negative). I draw both and they meet at (2, 3). I report the full point, x and y — the solution is (2, 3), not just 'x = 2.'

canonical_error.pattern: Graphs a negative-slope line going the wrong way (up instead of down), so the lines meet at the wrong point
canonical_error.example: For y = -x + 5, goes UP 1 for each step right instead of DOWN 1, so it crosses y = 2x - 1 somewhere other than the true point (2, 3)
canonical_error.why: A negative slope falls as you move right. Rising a negative-slope line shifts the whole line, moving the intersection to a point that solves neither original equation.

skills.name: Determine the solution of a system given its equations
skills.i_do_script: The solution to a system is the one point sitting on BOTH lines at once -- the single shared row in both lines' value columns. That is why a candidate point has to be checked against both equations, never just one, and never by eye. When I am given a system and asked which point (or which graph) is the solution, I find the crossing point and then CONFIRM it by substituting into both equations. Watch y = -2/3 x + 3 and y = 4/3 x - 3. Setting them equal, the lines cross at (3, 1). I check: -2/3 times 3 plus 3 = 1, and 4/3 times 3 minus 3 = 1 — both work, so (3, 1) is the solution. A point like (1, 3) with the coordinates reversed would fail both, so I never pick a point without testing it.

canonical_error.pattern: Selects a solution or a graph by matching a labeled point without substituting it back, so coordinate swaps or sign flips slip through
canonical_error.example: For y = -2/3 x + 3 and y = 4/3 x - 3 (solution (3, 1)), the student picks (1, 3) — the coordinates reversed — because it 'looks right'
canonical_error.why: The true solution must satisfy both equations. Testing (3, 1) passes both; testing the reversed (1, 3) fails both. Substituting is what rules out swapped or sign-flipped points.

skills.item_template: A system in y = mx + b form (possibly with candidate solutions or candidate graphs). Student determines the solution and confirms by substitution. MC.

sample_items.stem: What is the solution to this system?  y = -2/3x + 3  and  y = 4/3x - 3
sample_items.distractor_logic: Only (3, 1) satisfies both: -2/3(3) + 3 = 1 and 4/3(3) - 3 = 1. The others are coordinate swaps or sign flips that fail the check.

sample_items.stem: What is the solution to this system?  y = 2x - 4  and  y = -x + 2
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2(2) - 4 = 0 and -(2) + 2 = 0, so (2, 0). (0, 2) reverses the coordinates.

sample_items.stem: What is the solution to this system?  y = -3x + 5  and  y = x - 3
sample_items.distractor_logic: -3(2) + 5 = -1 and 2 - 3 = -1, so (2, -1). (-1, 2) swaps; (2, 1) flips the sign of y.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/2(2) + 2 = 3 and 2(2) - 1 = 3, so (2, 3). (3, 2) reverses it; the others flip signs.

redirect_script.prompt: Picture the two value columns: the solution is the one row BOTH columns agree on -- does your point actually sit in both? Don't pick a point because it looks right — test it. Put the x and y into BOTH equations. The real solution makes both true; a reversed or sign-flipped point will fail. If it fails either one, it's not the answer.
redirect_script.praise: You confirmed the point in both equations before choosing — that's how you rule out swaps and sign errors.

vocabulary.definition: Find the point where the lines cross and confirm it works in both equations.

worked_example_script.text: List both lines' heights at x = 0, 1, 2: y = -3x + 5 gives 5, 2, -1 and y = x - 3 gives -3, -2, -1.
At which x do the two columns agree? So what point do both lines pass through?

At x = 2 both columns say -1, so both lines pass through (2, -1) -- that is what 'solution' means: the one point on BOTH lines. The reversed pair (-1, 2) appears in neither column, so it cannot be the answer no matter how right it looks.
Write 'Which is the solution to y = -3x + 5 and y = x - 3: (2, -1) or (-1, 2)?'
Let's test (2, -1) first. What does each equation give?
-3(2) + 5 = -1 and 2 - 3 = -1 — both true, so (2, -1). Testing (-1, 2) fails both, so it's out.
If a student picks (-1, 2), ask 'does it make BOTH equations true? Substitute and see.'
Your turn: find the solution to y = 2x - 4 and y = -x + 2 and confirm it.

skills.name: Interpret and estimate the solution of a real-world system
skills.i_do_script: In a real-world system, each line is an option — like two price plans — and the point where they cross is the break-even point, where both options cost the same. Watch: Gym A is y = 10x + 30 (a $30 join fee plus $10 a month) and Gym B is y = 20x ($20 a month, no fee). They cross at (3, 60): at 3 months both cost $60. Before 3 months, Gym B (lower starting cost) is cheaper; after 3 months, Gym A (lower monthly rate) is cheaper. I read the crossing AND explain what it means.

canonical_error.pattern: Interprets the intersection or the 'better deal' backwards — assuming the option that starts higher (or lower) is always the more expensive one
canonical_error.example: Two plans meet at (3, 60). The student says Gym A (higher starting cost) is always more expensive, missing that after 3 months Gym A becomes the cheaper option
canonical_error.why: The intersection is the break-even point where costs are equal. Before it, the option with the lower starting value is cheaper; after it, the option with the lower rate (slope) is cheaper — the advantage switches at the crossing.

skills.item_template: A real-world system in y = mx + b form (with a graph or description). Student estimates the intersection and interprets it as a break-even point. Multi-part.

sample_items.stem: Gym A charges a $30 join fee plus $10 per month: y = 10x + 30. Gym B charges $20 per month with no fee: y = 20x. At how many months do they cost the same, and which is cheaper after that?
sample_items.answer: They cost the same at 3 months ($60). After 3 months Gym A is cheaper (lower monthly rate).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Crossing at (3, 60). Saying A is 'always more expensive' ignores that its lower rate wins after the break-even point.

sample_items.stem: Company A charges $50 up front plus $5 per hour: y = 5x + 50. Company B charges $15 per hour: y = 15x. When is the cost equal, and who is cheaper before that time?
sample_items.answer: Equal at 5 hours ($75). Before 5 hours, Company B is cheaper (no up-front cost).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Crossing at (5, 75). Before break-even, the lower starting cost (B) wins; after, A's lower rate wins.

sample_items.stem: Ava has $50 and saves $10 per week: y = 10x + 50. Ben has $20 and saves $16 per week: y = 16x + 20. In how many weeks will they have the same amount?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Crossing at (5, 100). Ben starts lower but saves faster, catching up at week 5.

sample_items.stem: Plan A costs $40 plus $2 per gigabyte: y = 2x + 40. Plan B costs $20 plus $6 per gigabyte: y = 6x + 20. At what usage are the costs equal, and which plan is better for heavy users (more gigabytes)?
sample_items.answer: Equal at 5 gigabytes ($50). For heavy users (more than 5 GB), Plan A is better (lower rate per GB).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Crossing at (5, 50). Above break-even the lower-rate plan (A) wins; below it, B's lower base wins.

redirect_script.praise: You read the break-even point and explained who wins before and after — that's interpreting the system.

The per-unit cost (per month, hour, GB); the steeper line costs more per unit.
The starting cost when x = 0, such as a fee or up-front charge.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for AI.SEI.2 (solve systems of linear equations algebraically and by graphing).

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, graphing a system from y = mx + b form and naming the intersection, the At-proficiency core. If they pass, move up to S5 (determine and confirm the solution from equations) and S6 (interpret a real-world system). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks graphing a proportional relationship as a line through the origin, and B2 checks solving two-step equations, the two grade 7 skills that graphing and verifying systems lean on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (plotting points) and F2 (substitution as a truth test) locate the gap in grades 5 and 6. S1, S2, and S3 remain available to probe counting solutions, checking a point in both equations, and reading an intersection off a given graph.
